canonicalRecord.finding_label: Upstream donor routes regenerate methionine for SAMe synthesis
canonicalRecord.finding_summary: Folate-dependent methionine synthase and betaine-dependent BHMT regenerate methionine from homocysteine. Choline can supply betaine. MAT then uses methionine and ATP to form SAMe.
canonicalRecord.finding_interpretation: This establishes connected precursor provision. It does not make folate, betaine or choline MAT reactants, demonstrate that more intake raises synthesis, or resolve a donor-inadequacy constraint on MAT capacity.
canonicalRecord.finding_statement: Folate and betaine remethylation regenerate methionine upstream of MAT-dependent SAMe formation; choline can contribute through betaine.
canonicalRecord.synthesis: Existing reviewed PM1-F1, PM2-F1/PM2-F2 and PM3-F1 establish the successive reaction identities. Folate provides 5-methyltetrahydrofolate for B12-dependent methionine synthase, while betaine supplies the alternative BHMT reaction, predominantly in liver and kidney. Choline oxidation can supply betaine. The regenerated methionine is available to the MAT reaction. Evidence supports the route, without requiring each donor to act directly on MAT.
canonicalRecord.synthesis_limitations: Tissue expression, alternative methionine supply and pathway compensation limit generalisation. SAMe and SAM:SAH are pool-state measurements rather than isolated synthesis rates. No established limiting effect on MAT capacity or nutrient-replete intake benefit is claimed.

canonicalRecord.finding_label: Upstream donor routes regenerate methionine for SAMe synthesis
canonicalRecord.finding_summary: Folate-dependent methionine synthase and betaine-dependent BHMT regenerate methionine from homocysteine. Choline can supply betaine. MAT then uses methionine and ATP to form SAMe.
canonicalRecord.finding_interpretation: This establishes connected precursor provision. It does not make folate, betaine or choline MAT reactants, demonstrate that more intake raises synthesis, or resolve a donor-inadequacy constraint on MAT capacity.
canonicalRecord.finding_statement: Folate and betaine remethylation regenerate methionine upstream of MAT-dependent SAMe formation; choline can contribute through betaine.
canonicalRecord.synthesis: Existing reviewed PM1-F1, PM2-F1/PM2-F2 and PM3-F1 establish the successive reaction identities. Folate provides 5-methyltetrahydrofolate for B12-dependent methionine synthase, while betaine supplies the alternative BHMT reaction, predominantly in liver and kidney. Choline oxidation can supply betaine. The regenerated methionine is available to the MAT reaction. Evidence supports the route, without requiring each donor to act directly on MAT.
canonicalRecord.synthesis_limitations: Tissue expression, alternative methionine supply and pathway compensation limit generalisation. SAMe and SAM:SAH are pool-state measurements rather than isolated synthesis rates. No established limiting effect on MAT capacity or nutrient-replete intake benefit is claimed.

record.title: MAT2B and MAT2A stability — proposed Finding
record.proposition: MAT2B association can preserve MAT2A protein or catalytic stability in purified-human-enzyme and mammalian-cell experiments. This supports a stability contribution to enzyme regulation, not an exclusive explanation of MAT2B action or a demonstrated increase in human SAMe synthesis flux.
record.capRationale: No existing cap triggered by Directness 2, Bias Protection 1, Precision 1 and Replication 1. Raw and adjusted 5/8. No extra decrement for model boundaries.
record.scopeNote: Preview-only proposed synthesis of an experimental component already present in F1's supporting evidence, with independently recovered cellular corroboration. Not a canonical Finding or dietary lever. Activity preservation and protein stability are related but non-identical endpoints.

rationale.D: Both experiments directly test the explicitly model-bounded stability proposition. No bridge to human brain flux or nutritional response is included; those propositions are excluded rather than silently scored.
rationale.B: Orthogonal activity readouts, protein identity/binding assays, cell depletion/knockout and wild-type/mutant rescue offer meaningful protection. Representative blots, limited independently quantified preparation counts and incompletely reported masking retain Bias Protection 1; these are not proof of a critical flaw.
rationale.P: Activity-decay time courses and protein-chase contrasts support a stability contribution. Cellular results are largely representative repeated blots, with no harmonised stability effect interval across models. Precision 1 concerns magnitude and boundary uncertainty, not an invented sample-size threshold.
rationale.R: The Bailey and 2024 cell-study author groups are separate; both support a stability contribution using different models/endpoints. This is partial independent corroboration, not two exact-endpoint replications. Replication 1, not 2. Independent replication was not established in this assessment. This qualification concerns an identical model and stability endpoint, not the verified partial corroboration.

limitations: Partial cross-model corroboration does not quantify MAT2B-dependent stability or SAMe flux in the human brain.
Does not establish that stability is the only MAT2B mechanism: allosteric/catalytic interpretations remain relevant.
No dietary methionine, folate, betaine, choline or ADHD intervention effect was assessed.

sources.contradictoryAssessment: No experiment falsifying the scoped stability contribution was verified. Alternative catalytic/allosteric mechanisms challenge an exclusive stability-only claim, which is explicitly not the assessed proposition.

targetedChecks.access: Scite full text; enzyme-assay Methods, inhibition, binding and stability Results appraised
targetedChecks.assessment: Purified human MAT2A lost activity during substrate-free incubation at 37 C; MAT2B preserved activity. Coupled phosphate and direct LC-MS assays distinguish stability from steady-state kinetic effects. Activity half-life about 2.3 minutes without MAT2B; activity retained over the 120-minute experiment with MAT2B. Technical repeats do not constitute independent replication.

targetedChecks.role: Independent partial corroboration of protein stability
targetedChecks.access: Scite full text; cell perturbation/rescue Results and cycloheximide-chase Methods appraised
targetedChecks.assessment: Separate research group: depletion, knockout and wild-type versus binding-domain-mutant rescue support MAT2B-dependent MAT2A protein stability in mammalian cell models. Protein abundance/chase differs from purified-enzyme activity decay. Mostly representative blots with two or three repeats; no pooled half-life or universal flux effect is claimed. Later tumour/diet experiments do not establish a nutritional PM recommendation.

targetedChecks.role: Contextual structural/allosteric interpretation; challenges stability-only explanations
targetedChecks.access: Scite full-text conformational Results, Discussion and construct Methods appraised
targetedChecks.assessment: CryoEM conformers suggest additional allosteric regulation. Catalytic-activity arguments partly reuse earlier experiments; this is not independent replication of the stability endpoint. Does not refute a stability contribution or establish that all MAT2B effects are stability alone.

targetedChecks.role: Contradictory substrate-order model; contextual to stability
targetedChecks.access: Scite full-text human MAT2A kinetic Results appraised
targetedChecks.assessment: Steady-state, stopped-flow and isotope-exchange evidence supports rapid-equilibrium random substrate binding, conflicting with Bailey's ATP-first model. Retained as a distinct unresolved kinetic issue, not evidence against MAT2B-mediated stability.

retrievalLimited.limitation: Publisher retrieval failed; legitimate Scite full text recovered relevant Results and Methods. Raw immunoblot data and supplementary quantitative half-life reconstruction were not independently reanalysed; Precision remains 1.

record.stoppingRationale: Bounded recovery recovered load-bearing purified-enzyme and cell experiments, screened twelve forward citation edges (truncated discovery, not exhaustive), and examined a conflicting kinetic study and newer structural interpretation. Citation labels/counts were not treated as replication. Further broad retrieval is unlikely to change the model-bounded stability judgement materially.

history.decision: Version 1: proposed experimental Finding, Codex-assessed provisional 5/8; not human-reviewed. Original F1/F4 chemistry and source IDs preserved separately; no canonical admission.

record.title: Dietary protein delivers circulating phenylalanine; kinetics depend on context
record.proposition: Dietary protein supplies phenylalanine to the human circulation, with delivery kinetics varying by the tested protein source, dose and meal context. The pooled age association is context-dependent, not proof that ageing uniformly impairs absorption or that greater availability increases brain neurotransmitters.
record.capRationale: Directness 2, Bias Protection 1 and Precision 1: no D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies. Replication 0 receives no extra decrement.

rationale.D: Direct human dietary tracer appearance tests the specified supply process; concentration-only studies corroborate context, not exact flux.
rationale.B: Controlled isotope methods support supply, but pooled source/dose comparisons are not a single randomised contrast and age is observational. These are appraised residual concerns, not missing evidence automatically scored zero.
rationale.P: Measured appearance is informative, but reported variability and heterogeneous matrices permit materially different magnitudes; no universal age or dosage effect is asserted.
rationale.R: Independent source-response evidence partially corroborates the scoped claim; exact tracer/age/dose comparisons retain research-team dependence. Constituent pooled trials are not counted again.

limitations: Mostly male dairy-tracer cohorts; between-study source/dose contrasts, nonrandomised age comparisons and different matrices limit generalisation. No brain transport, neurotransmitter or ADHD endpoint.

Evidence-confidence conclusions must distinguish limitations of the underlying scientific evidence from limitations of the framework's evidence retrieval and assessment. Absence of verified evidence within an assessment must not be represented as evidence of absence.

sources.contradictoryAssessment: Supporting and null outcomes are endpoint-specific. No uniform age impairment is asserted; exercise and newer source studies qualify that inference.

targetedChecks.access: Full published PDF examined: abstract, data selection, tracer methods, statistics, results and limitations.
targetedChecks.assessment: Pooled 18 laboratory RCT datasets; 602 participants, 590 men; age is not randomised. Dietary tracer enters circulation; protein type and dose affect kinetics. Pooled older-younger difference is not universal age impairment. Five-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: 50% ± 14% overall; casein 45% ± 11%, whey 57% ± 10%, milk 65% ± 13% (means ± SD). Pooled older/young comparison: 45% ± 10% versus 51% ± 14%; not randomised age assignment. Reported variability and subgroup tests; interstudy comparisons and participant differences limit causal interpretation. One research programme; constituent trials and this pooled analysis must not be counted twice.

targetedChecks.role: supporting; contradicts a universal animal-over-plant hierarchy
targetedChecks.access: Scite full-text Methods and Results, including randomisation, washout, assays, power and multiplicity; published Cambridge PDF checked.
targetedChecks.assessment: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes. Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.  Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows. Independent of Maastricht pooled dairy corpus; age analyses and six visits within a person are not six independent replications.

targetedChecks.access: Published abstract and full institutional thesis chapter 2 examined.
targetedChecks.assessment: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total. Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.  Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence. NCT00557388 is part of Gorissen2020; no double-counting.

previousAssessments.title: Dietary protein delivers circulating phenylalanine; kinetics depend on context
previousAssessments.proposition: Dietary protein supplies phenylalanine to the human circulation, with delivery kinetics varying by the tested protein source, dose and meal context. The pooled age association is context-dependent, not proof that ageing uniformly impairs absorption or that greater availability increases brain neurotransmitters.
previousAssessments.capRationale: Directness 2, Bias Protection 1 and Precision 1: no D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies. Replication 0 receives no extra decrement.

rationale.D: Direct human dietary tracer appearance tests the specified supply process; concentration-only studies corroborate context, not exact flux.
rationale.B: Controlled isotope methods support supply, but pooled source/dose comparisons are not a single randomised contrast and age is observational. These are appraised residual concerns, not missing evidence automatically scored zero.
rationale.P: Measured appearance is informative, but reported variability and heterogeneous matrices permit materially different magnitudes; no universal age or dosage effect is asserted.
rationale.R: Independent source-response evidence partially corroborates the scoped claim; exact tracer/age/dose comparisons retain research-team dependence. Constituent pooled trials are not counted again.

limitations: Mostly male dairy-tracer cohorts; between-study source/dose contrasts, nonrandomised age comparisons and different matrices limit generalisation. No brain transport, neurotransmitter or ADHD endpoint.

targetedChecks.access: Full published PDF examined: abstract, data selection, tracer methods, statistics, results and limitations.
targetedChecks.assessment: Pooled 18 laboratory RCT datasets; 602 participants, 590 men; age is not randomised. Dietary tracer enters circulation; protein type and dose affect kinetics. Pooled older-younger difference is not universal age impairment. Five-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: 50% ± 14% overall; casein 45% ± 11%, whey 57% ± 10%, milk 65% ± 13% (means ± SD). Pooled older/young comparison: 45% ± 10% versus 51% ± 14%; not randomised age assignment. Reported variability and subgroup tests; interstudy comparisons and participant differences limit causal interpretation. One research programme; constituent trials and this pooled analysis must not be counted twice.

targetedChecks.assessment: Independent Exeter programme; randomised double-blind six-period crossover, 12 young and 10 older adults, both sexes. Source-specific plasma profiles; some non-animal sources produced higher essential-amino-acid responses than the tested milk beverage. Integrated responses did not show a uniform age decrement.  Small cohorts; composition and food matrix differ, so no isolated digestibility estimate or universal ranking follows. Independent of Maastricht pooled dairy corpus; age analyses and six visits within a person are not six independent replications.

targetedChecks.access: Published abstract and full institutional thesis chapter 2 examined.
targetedChecks.assessment: Young/older men, rest/exercise comparisons; 48 participants total. Dietary phenylalanine availability did not differ detectably with exercise although muscle incorporation increased.  Muscle utilisation is not circulating-pool enhancement; a nonsignificant contrast is not equivalence. NCT00557388 is part of Gorissen2020; no double-counting.

record.title: Mincing changed dietary phenylalanine appearance in older men
record.proposition: In a randomised crossover study of ten older men, 135 g minced beef produced greater six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance than the same quantity of steak. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably between preparations.
record.capRationale: Directness 2, Bias Protection 1 and Precision 1: no D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies. Replication 0 receives no extra decrement.

rationale.D: Same-cut beef and isotope-labelled dietary phenylalanine directly test the exact older-men preparation proposition.
rationale.B: Randomised within-person design and matched source/quantity reduce confounding. Visible texture and consumption-time differences remain; concealment and assay masking were not demonstrated in recovered methods. No critical systematic error was established.
rationale.P: Reported tracer effect and standard errors support the directional finding, but n=10, no extracted paired interval and negative secondary outcomes limit magnitude and extrapolation; nulls are not scored as equivalence.
rationale.R: The bounded exact-protocol search and source appraisal yielded one empirical dataset; thesis/journal reports and other processing studies are not independent replications. Independent replication was not established in this assessment.

limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

Evidence-confidence conclusions must distinguish limitations of the underlying scientific evidence from limitations of the framework's evidence retrieval and assessment. Absence of verified evidence within an assessment must not be represented as evidence of absence.

sources.contradictoryAssessment: Supporting and null outcomes are endpoint-specific. No detected total-amino-acid or muscle-synthesis advantage in the same experiment.

targetedChecks.access: Published abstract plus full experimental chapter 6 in the author institutional thesis; final published quantitative result cross-checked against author-shared publication.
targetedChecks.assessment: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart. More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably. Six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: minced 61% ± 3% versus steak 49% ± 3% (means ± SEM), P < 0.01; 12 percentage-point difference. No paired confidence interval calculated or inferred. Small single trial; mean estimates and standard errors available, paired effect interval not extracted; no equivalence claim for null outcomes. Single empirical dataset; thesis and journal article are the same experiment, not replications.

Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably between preparations.
record.capRationale: Directness 2, Bias Protection 1 and Precision 1: no D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies. Replication 0 receives no extra decrement.

rationale.D: Same-cut beef and isotope-labelled dietary phenylalanine directly test the exact older-men preparation proposition.
rationale.B: Randomised within-person design and matched source/quantity reduce confounding. Visible texture and consumption-time differences remain; concealment and assay masking were not demonstrated in recovered methods. No critical systematic error was established.
rationale.P: Reported tracer effect and standard errors support the directional finding, but n=10, no extracted paired interval and negative secondary outcomes limit magnitude and extrapolation; nulls are not scored as equivalence.
rationale.R: The bounded exact-protocol search and source appraisal yielded one empirical dataset; thesis/journal reports and other processing studies are not independent replications. Independent replication was not established in this assessment.

limitations: One small older-male trial; no independent replication of the exact matched-beef protocol was established in this assessment. No claim that all foods should be minced or that this improves attention.

Evidence-confidence conclusions must distinguish limitations of the underlying scientific evidence from limitations of the framework's evidence retrieval and assessment. Absence of verified evidence within an assessment must not be represented as evidence of absence.

Intervention disposition: the matched 135 g lean-beef preparation experiment in ten older men remains scientific evidence only. No approved canonical preparation SOP or food-strategy registration is established; exact intervention scope awaits confirmation.

sources.contradictoryAssessment: Supporting and null outcomes are endpoint-specific. No detected total-amino-acid or muscle-synthesis advantage in the same experiment.

targetedChecks.access: Published abstract plus full experimental chapter 6 in the author institutional thesis; final published quantitative result cross-checked against author-shared publication.
targetedChecks.assessment: Randomised crossover; ten older men, mean age 74 years; two visits at least 14 days apart. More dietary phenylalanine appeared after mincing. Total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle synthesis did not differ detectably. Six-hour dietary phenylalanine appearance: minced 61% ± 3% versus steak 49% ± 3% (means ± SEM), P < 0.01; 12 percentage-point difference. No paired confidence interval calculated or inferred. Small single trial; mean estimates and standard errors available, paired effect interval not extracted; no equivalence claim for null outcomes. Single empirical dataset; thesis and journal article are the same experiment, not replications.

record.title: Extrusion altered early amino-acid kinetics, not demonstrated total loss
record.proposition: In a randomised crossover of nine healthy young adults, the tested high-moisture-extruded mycoprotein/pea blend delayed selected early plasma amino-acid responses relative to the dry blend. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different; the study does not establish poorer overall nutrition for all meat alternatives.
record.capRationale: Directness 2, Bias Protection 1 and Precision 1: no D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies. Replication 0 receives no extra decrement.

rationale.D: The claim is explicitly about measured plasma kinetics in the exact human crossover, not absolute absorption or clinical efficacy.
rationale.B: Randomised counterbalanced double-blind visits and analytical measurement support inference; n=9 and numerous endpoints with residual matrix differences warrant caution, not an invented critical-bias judgement.
rationale.P: Direction of selected early responses is resolved, but null integrated areas lack equivalence bounds; scope excludes a demonstrated total loss.
rationale.R: One matched-product experimental line was assessed. The same group's different protein-source trial and technical in-vitro repeats do not replicate this exact intervention; independent replication was not established in this assessment.

limitations: Single small trial, no dietary tracer, numerous secondary endpoints and laboratory reconstituted products. Not proof of equal total absorption or a reason to avoid all processed plant foods.

Evidence-confidence conclusions must distinguish limitations of the underlying scientific evidence from limitations of the framework's evidence retrieval and assessment. Absence of verified evidence within an assessment must not be represented as evidence of absence.

sources.contradictoryAssessment: Supporting and null outcomes are endpoint-specific. No significant total five-hour grouped exposure difference; not evidence of equivalence.

targetedChecks.role: supporting for kinetic change; null integrated outcomes
targetedChecks.access: Scite full-text human methods, composition, power/statistics and results examined.
targetedChecks.assessment: Randomised double-blind counterbalanced crossover; nine young adults, five men/four women; minimum five-day separation. Extrusion delayed early responses and reduced selected peaks, including phenylalanine and tyrosine. Total five-hour grouped amino-acid availability was not significantly different. Phenylalanine peak: dry blend 72 ± 3 versus extruded 58 ± 3 micromol/L, P=0.020; time to peak 32 ± 4 versus 83 ± 20 minutes, P=0.037 (means ± SEM). Total five-hour grouped amino-acid iAUC: no statistically significant difference; no equivalence bounds inferred. Small single dataset; no tracer, many endpoints, uncertainty on paired differences; laboratory reconstituted products not every commercial meat alternative. Distinct study but same Exeter programme as nonanimal2024; not an independent replication of its six-source comparison.

record.capRationale: D2: no inferential cap for the plasma proposition. No B0/P0 cap applies. R1 limits replication credit; no extra deduction.

rationale.D: 2/2: controlled feeding studies measure the scoped plasma ratio directly. Human brain uptake and benefit are explicitly excluded.
rationale.B: 1/2: Wurtman randomised meal order, used objective assays and order-adjusted/multiplicity-aware analysis. Visible meals, one incomplete participant and incompletely established protections in historical and protein-source studies leave residual concerns; no critical bias is demonstrated.
rationale.P: 1/2: source-specific contrasts and reported SEM/ranges distinguish a meal effect in tested conditions. Small samples, heterogeneous protocols and limited paired uncertainty leave materially different magnitudes and boundaries plausible. Null experiments are not equivalence results.
rationale.R: 1/2: separate investigator groups and datasets corroborate plasma meal responsiveness, but protocol/denominator differences and credible evening/starch nulls preclude full replication credit. This is not independent replication of one exact meal protocol.

limitations: Small acute healthy-adult samples; different meals, ratio denominators and sampling windows; incomplete historical methods retrieval. No population-wide optimum or direct human brain-flux estimate. Evening null results limit generalisation but are not equivalence evidence.

record.title: Mitochondrial oxidant production is source- and state-dependent
record.proposition: Specific mitochondrial electron-transfer sites generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; source-specific suppression can reduce oxidant production without inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation. Succinate oxidation during reperfusion can drive excessive production through reverse electron transport.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: Brand site-selective suppressors and Chouchani reperfusion perturbations test source generation, respiration and reverse-electron-transport endpoints in the stated experimental models (Brand Figs 1–2, 5; Chouchani Figs 2–4). No food or human efficacy proposition is scored.
rationale.B: Source counterscreens and respiration controls limit nonspecific inhibition, and reperfusion experiments add tracer/pharmacological checks. Tool selectivity and between-model transfer remain material residual concerns; this is not a fully bias-protected dietary trial.
rationale.P: Dose-response/selectivity and respiratory measurements discriminate source suppression from generalized inhibition. The limits of selectivity and translation across preparations leave uncertainty in effect size and applicable source boundaries; P2 is not established.
rationale.R: The two research programmes provide partially matching evidence for source-dependent complex-I oxidant regulation. They do not independently replicate every component of this composite Finding; multiple models within Brand are not counted as independent research-group replication.

record.capRationale: No D1/B0/P0 ceiling applies; adjusted equals raw. No extra model-to-human penalty is added because the proposition remains model-specific.
limitations: Experimental suppressors and ischaemia models establish source regulation, not dietary effectiveness. These results do not imply that all mitochondrial ROS are harmful or that mitochondrial emission assays isolate gross production.

record.title: High-fat exposure altered mitochondrial H2O2-emitting potential
record.proposition: A specified high-fat meal and short high-fat feeding period increased skeletal-muscle mitochondrial H2O2-emitting potential in a small human experiment; separate rodent perturbations supported a role for mitochondrial oxidants in insulin resistance.
record.process: Codex bounded PM4/PM5 SEC completion v1: exact propositions, primary full-text recovery, factor-specific appraisal, scoped independence and explicit unresolved judgements; no human scientific-review status inferred.

methodology.name: Existing SEC four-factor anchors and integrated caps

rationale.D: Anderson Fig. 6 tests the specified meal/short-feeding exposure and human muscle H2O2 emission. Its separate rodent interventions support the separately stated rodent clause, not human mediation.
rationale.B: Within-person baseline and validated emission/respirometry assays help attribution, but the sequential human feeding design lacks a randomized contemporaneous meal comparator; diet/time/order confounding remains. The scored statement is the observed experiment, not a causal replacement-diet claim.
rationale.P: Fig. 6 reports participant-level/sample-size context, mean/SEM and group comparisons; the rise is informative for the tested exposure. Nine men, assay-specific conditions and uncertain magnitude beyond this sample preclude P2. Rodent effects are not pooled with human precision.
rationale.R: Only one independent human feeding dataset supports the exact meal/five-day muscle-emission result in the bounded assessed body. The obese cross-section and rodent arms do not replicate that exposure/population proposition. R0 describes this scoped body, not proof of absence throughout the literature.

record.proposition: Competition and functional acclimation can change community glycan processing even when several organisms possess relevant utilisation genes.
record.canonicalProposition: Competition and functional acclimation can change community glycan processing even when several organisms possess relevant utilisation genes.

rationale.D: Direct gene-fitness, proteomic and in vivo degradation measurements test the scoped community-processing proposition; no human clinical inference is required.
rationale.B: Orthogonal assays, omission controls, germ-free controls and spike-in controls protect the mechanism. Allocation/blinding are not established and selected defined communities, strain differences and proteomic imputation leave residual concerns; no demonstrated critical flaw warrants B0.
rationale.P: Calibrated GC-MS with controls and 95% intervals distinguishes residual from lost arabinoxylan degradation. Small animal groups and glycan/context-dependent compensation leave material uncertainty about magnitude and scope, precluding P2.
rationale.R: Patnode is the one fully appraised empirical line for the exact combined competition/acclimation/degradation proposition. Sonnenburg and Rakoff confirm related resource-context effects but not that exact degradation outcome; Desai tests resource substitution, not competitor-dependent compensation. Multiple assays within Patnode are not independent replication.

limitations: Defined mouse communities do not establish a universal human response, benefit from greater diversity or an optimal turnover rate. Substrate use can also accompany adverse host effects. Specific SCFA, polyphenol and precursor conversions belong to PM5, PM6 and PM8.
Assessment is provisional and not qualified-human reviewed. SEC does not establish dietary efficacy or alter admissions.

targetedChecks.access: NCBI BioC full article, Results, Methods and Figure 7 legends (PMC2900928), retrieved 2026-11-02.
targetedChecks.assessment: Genetic complementation and inulin gain-of-function tested alongside defined two-species mouse communities. B. caccae rose from approximately 13% to 51% on the inulin-only polysaccharide diet (n=7); the B. vulgatus comparison was imprecise (n=3, p=0.1). Lower-dose inulin in a polysaccharide-rich diet gave no detected advantage, but on a polysaccharide-free diet B. caccae rose 26±8 percentage points. Inulin-enabled Bt removed the B. caccae advantage. Do not isolate dose from competing substrates or infer a universal human benefit.

record.proposition: High-fibre intake can increase metagenomic glycan-processing potential without increased diversity, while fermented-food-associated immune changes do not establish diversity-mediated benefit.
record.canonicalProposition: High-fibre intake can increase metagenomic glycan-processing potential without increased diversity, while fermented-food-associated immune changes do not establish diversity-mediated benefit.

rationale.D: The proposition explicitly concerns encoded processing potential and the absence of a demonstrated mediation claim. Shotgun CAZymes and diversity directly address those endpoints; no actual flux or immune benefit mediated by diversity is asserted.
rationale.B: Prospective allocation, longitudinal sampling and multiplicity adjustment offer protection. Two nonrandom allocations, unblinded conduct, exclusions, no untreated arm and exploratory outcomes leave residual bias. The scoped potential/association statement avoids a strong comparative therapeutic claim.
rationale.P: Eleven increased CAZyme families narrow the encoded-potential inference. The small cohort, exploratory uncertainty and absence of equivalence testing prevent treating stable diversity or null primary immunity as proof of no possible effect; P1 rather than P2.
rationale.R: One human cohort supports this exact joint proposition. Repeated samples, omics platforms and diet arms are not independent replication. The later trial differs in exposure/endpoints and does not establish independent confirmation of the joint CAZyme/diversity result.

limitations: The prespecified cytokine-response score did not change. Gene abundance is functional potential, not enzyme flux; stool metabolite concentration is not production rate. Diversity and immune changes were accompanying results, not demonstrated causal mediation. No improvement in cognition surveys, glucose, lipids or blood pressure was established.
Assessment is provisional and not qualified-human reviewed. SEC does not establish dietary efficacy or alter admissions.

record.proposition: Inulin utilisation machinery changed microbial competitive responses to dietary inulin in defined communities.
record.canonicalProposition: Inulin utilisation machinery changed microbial competitive responses to dietary inulin in defined communities.

rationale.D: Gain-of-function and genetic perturbation plus diet-dependent competition directly test the defined-community inulin proposition, without a bridge to human benefit.
rationale.B: Genetic complementation, strain-specific qPCR and defined diet/community contrasts reduce causal ambiguity. Small groups, allocation/blinding not established and partly entangled dose/background-polysaccharide contrasts leave residual concerns.
rationale.P: Figure 7 differentiates a clear B. caccae advantage and its loss after inulin use is conferred on Bt. Small groups (3–7), the non-significant B. vulgatus contrast and diet-context variability prevent a precise general competitive effect or P2.
rationale.R: Rakoff-Nahoum independently confirms that inulin-handling genes alter community-dependent fitness. Different species, loci and cooperative rather than identical competitive comparisons support R1, not R2. The elderly human composition study does not replicate genetic mechanism; the newer preprint is contextual only.

limitations: Effects depend on utilisation genes, dose and competing glycans. Inulin in a polysaccharide-rich diet did not give the same competitive advantage. No guaranteed butyrate response or health benefit. 16S abundance is not measured glycan-processing flux; this formulated ingredient is not an ordinary vegetable intervention. Immune endpoints were unchanged.
Assessment is provisional and not qualified-human reviewed. SEC does not establish dietary efficacy or alter admissions.

record.capRationale: No ceiling applies to D2/B1/P1/R1; provisional 5/8 for the scoped transport proposition, not a dietary efficacy score.

rationale.D: Direct tracer competition in rat BBB experiments and selective transport after LAT1/4F2hc co-expression address the experimental transport proposition. Human meal efficacy is outside the claim; molecular structures are corroboration, not clinical transport measurements.
rationale.B: Internal controls include reference tracer and efflux checks in the rat experiment, subunit-alone/water controls and ion/substrate comparisons in expression experiments. These support interpretation, but the small experiments do not establish random allocation or blinded analysis; residual model and assay concerns remain.
rationale.P: Concentration-response data and reported replicate variability resolve the direction of competition and selective transport. Small animal groups and oocyte assays do not establish precise cross-model physiological effect sizes or human net flux; precision is bounded rather than high.
rationale.R: Rat competition and independent Kanai expression work converge across methods. Boado shares the Pardridge investigator lineage and uses a related oocyte approach; these are not counted as fully independent replications of the complete BBB proposition. Structural corroboration is not transport replication.

limitations: Rat BBB transport, heterologous molecular function and human protein structure are distinct evidence levels; none establishes an ordinary-meal effect on human brain flux or cognition.
The 1975 paper and Yan 2019 remain abstract/record-level checks; the numerical appraisal rests on accessible experimental methods, not assumed methods in those reports.
Plasma ratios omit intracellular exchange conditions and do not measure net BBB uptake.

record.title: Phenylalanine conversion and endogenous tyrosine supply
record.proposition: Human tracer studies demonstrate endogenous conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine and a contribution to circulating tyrosine supply. This physiological supply relationship is distinct from PAH reaction identity and does not establish a dietary dose, brain uptake or catecholamine response.
record.capRationale: Existing D/B/P/R sum and ceilings applied; no extra replication decrement.

rationale.D: Regional human tracer conversion and net tyrosine release directly test the bounded endogenous-supply proposition, not meal efficacy.
rationale.B: Møller used screened volunteers, standardised prior diet, verified catheter positions, calibrated isotope assays and steady-state checks. Separate regional cohorts and uncertain intracellular precursor enrichment leave residual model bias; no causal diet comparison is claimed.
rationale.P: Tracer gradients and reported SEM resolve conversion and net release in the tested sample, but small cohorts and intracellular enrichment assumptions limit magnitudes and organ fractions.
rationale.R: Tessari provides independent-sample and independent-team regional tracer corroboration. Abstract-only access and differences in normalisation prevent full replication credit; reviews are not extra datasets.

targetedChecks.assessment: Dual tracers, renal/splanchnic catheterisation, calibration and isotope plateaus support conversion. Intracellular enrichment limits organ fractions.

targetedChecks.assessment: Regional isotope approach corroborates conversion; full controls and uncertainty not credited.

title: Acetylcholine Synthesis Support
pm_id: BRS1-FM2-PM6
mission: 'Maintain the capacity to form acetylcholine so cholinergic signalling for attention, working memory, and learning stays supplied.'
parent_fm: BRS1(FM2)
parent_brs: BRS1
summary: 'Acetylcholine is made in nerve endings when choline is joined to acetyl-CoA, a cell-made acetate carrier. Diet can provide choline itself or choline from phosphatidylcholine, and vitamin B5 supports the acetyl-CoA side. Entry into the nerve ending still controls access to the reaction. The reaction supplies acetylcholine for later cholinergic signalling.'

intervention_breakdown: Food-State Dominant
timing_specific: 'Yes'

    dietary_input: true

    evidence_source:

scientific_findings_intro: 'Transporter evidence identifies terminal choline uptake as a control step for acetylcholine synthesis, while human tracing demonstrates systemic assimilation of choline from dietary phosphatidylcholine. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Animal depletion and rescue studies support bounded pantothenate and one-carbon dependencies, with acetylcholine responses varying by experimental condition, region and age. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) The evidence therefore supports provision and local synthesis capacity without equating plasma choline delivery with neuronal release, attention benefit or a human dose response.'
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM6-F1
    finding_label: High-affinity choline uptake controls substrate entry into cholinergic terminals
    finding_summary: The high-affinity choline transporter recovers choline into cholinergic nerve endings and is a major control point for acetylcholine production.
    finding_interpretation: 'Substrate supply is not only a food-intake question: choline must reach the nerve terminal through a regulated transporter before choline acetyltransferase can use it.'
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: Sodium-coupled high-affinity choline uptake through CHT/SLC5A7 is required to recover choline into cholinergic nerve terminals and commonly limits acetylcholine production under physiological demand.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A focused transporter review shows that CHT recovers synaptic choline into cholinergic terminals, that inhibiting or genetically impairing this transport reduces cholinergic capacity, and that activity-dependent trafficking changes uptake capacity. This establishes terminal uptake as a control step upstream of the ChAT reaction.'
    synthesis_limitations: Transporter biology is largely mechanistic and preclinical. It does not show that ordinary choline intake changes CHT capacity in humans or that more dietary choline overcomes a transporter defect.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Ojiakor and Rylett (2020)
        citation_key: ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: CHT-mediated high-affinity choline uptake recovers choline into cholinergic terminals and is the principal regulated supply step for sustaining acetylcholine production.
        assessment:
          study: 'Review of CHT function, trafficking, genetic disruption, and pharmacological manipulation.'
          population: 'Cellular, animal, human genetic, and neuropathology evidence; not a dietary trial.'
          result: 'Reduced CHT function or availability limits choline uptake and cholinergic transmission, while neuronal activity recruits transport capacity.'
          effect_magnitude: No pooled dietary effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the regulated choline-entry step required before acetylcholine synthesis.
          limitations: Does not test ordinary food intake or human brain synthesis after a meal.
      - label: Xue et al. (2024)
        citation_key: xue_human_cht1_structure_2024
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#xue_human_cht1_structure_2024
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        exposure_context: Controlled transport substrates and ions; not a dietary salt experiment.
        directional_finding: Human CHT1 structures and transport-site mutations identify sodium-dependent choline uptake; chloride binding has a distinct functional role.
        assessment:
          study: Human CHT1 cryo-EM structures and uptake/site-mutant experiments.
          population: Human transporter expressed in experimental systems.
          result: Human CHT1 structures and transport-site mutations identify sodium-dependent choline uptake; chloride binding has a distinct functional role.
          effect_magnitude: No additional magnitude inferred.
          evidence_summary: Human CHT1 structures and transport-site mutations identify sodium-dependent choline uptake; chloride binding has a distinct functional role.
          limitations: Transport-ion capacity does not establish that added dietary salt increases brain choline uptake or acetylcholine output. CNS homeostasis and membrane gradients intervene. Chloride is not assumed to have identical transport stoichiometry and is not independently admitted here.
          retrieval_scope: Primary structural and transport results retrieved 26 October 2026.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Inazu (2019)
        citation_key: inazu_choline_transporters_2019
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#inazu_choline_transporters_2019
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: Separates CTL1/CTL2-mediated choline handling at brain microvascular endothelium from CHT/SLC5A7 uptake at cholinergic terminals.
        why_excluded: Does not test whether an oral choline exposure increases delivery to terminals or acetylcholine synthesis in humans.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F2
    finding_label: Choline and acetyl-CoA form acetylcholine via choline acetyltransferase
    finding_summary: Choline combines with acetyl-CoA through choline acetyltransferase to form acetylcholine. Necessity of those reactants is not proof that extra choline raises human brain acetylcholine.
    finding_interpretation: Choline and acetyl-CoA are the two substrates. Phosphatidylcholine and pantothenate matter through provision routes assessed separately; vitamin B12 and folate do not act as ChAT cofactors.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: Acetylcholine is formed from choline and acetyl-CoA by choline acetyltransferase; biochemical necessity is not intake-responsive human brain acetylcholine.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: A choline-acetyltransferase review and a modern choline-transporter review agree that ChAT transfers the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline in cholinergic neurons. Together they establish the defining reaction and both substrates.
    synthesis_limitations: 'Reaction and review evidence does not establish which substrate limits synthesis in every physiological state, an ordinary dietary dose response, or a human functional benefit.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Oda (1999)
        citation_key: oda_choline_1999
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#oda_choline_1999
        data_level: Mechanistic

        assessment:

          population: Experimental and neuropathology literature; not a dietary sample.
          result: Identified choline and acetyl-CoA as the enzyme’s substrates.
          effect_magnitude: No dietary or clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the acetylcholine-forming reaction.
          limitations: Enzyme and pathology review; not an intake-to-acetylcholine trial.
      - label: Ojiakor and Rylett (2020)
        citation_key: ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ojiakor_choline_transporter_2020
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: ChAT transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline in the neuronal cytoplasm after CHT-mediated choline entry.
        assessment:
          study: Review of CHT function and cholinergic terminal biology.
          population: 'Mechanistic, animal, and human genetic literature.'
          result: Describes substrate entry followed by ChAT-dependent synthesis from choline and acetyl-CoA.
          effect_magnitude: No dietary effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Independently confirms the reaction participants within the presynaptic synthesis pathway.
          limitations: Does not measure human synthesis after dietary exposure.
    evidence_dependency:

    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F4
    finding_label: Dietary phosphatidylcholine is a choline-provision route
    finding_summary: 'Phosphatidylcholine is a choline-containing dietary form that is digested, absorbed, and remodelled. It provides choline but is not a second substrate in the ChAT reaction.'
    finding_interpretation: 'Represent phosphatidylcholine as Derived provision to choline, not as an independent acetylcholine-synthesis requirement.'
    finding_statement: 'Dietary phosphatidylcholine is digested and remodelled into circulating phosphatidylcholine and free choline, establishing a dietary provision route to the direct choline substrate.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'In a randomized crossover tracer study in six healthy men, labelled phosphatidylcholine produced a delayed rise in labelled plasma choline and a larger phosphatidylcholine exposure than water-soluble choline forms. The tracer results directly establish digestion and systemic assimilation as a choline-containing dietary route.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Small single-dose study in healthy men. Plasma appearance does not measure delivery to cholinergic terminals, acetylcholine synthesis, neurotransmitter release, attention, or clinical benefit.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Böckmann et al. (2023)
        citation_key: bockmann_choline_supplements_2023
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#bockmann_choline_supplements_2023
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: isolated-substance
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Oral labelled phosphatidylcholine produced delayed circulating labelled choline and the highest labelled phosphatidylcholine exposure among four tested choline forms.
        assessment:
          study: Randomized crossover stable-isotope comparison of four oral choline forms.
          population: Six healthy adult men.
          result: 'Phosphatidylcholine was digested and remodelled, with delayed plasma choline appearance and higher plasma phosphatidylcholine exposure.'
          effect_magnitude: Delayed choline peak and approximately 2.3-fold higher peak labelled phosphatidylcholine than water-soluble forms.
          evidence_summary: Establishes phosphatidylcholine as an assimilated choline-provision route.
          limitations: Small sample; supplement bolus rather than whole food; no brain or acetylcholine measurement.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F5
    finding_label: Pantothenate supports the acetyl-CoA side of acetylcholine synthesis
    finding_summary: 'Pantothenate (vitamin B5) is needed to make coenzyme A, which cells use to form acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA supplies the acetyl group in acetylcholine.'
    finding_interpretation: 'Vitamin B5 is a biochemical precursor route to acetyl-CoA, not a ChAT cofactor or a second Direct Dietary Requirement. The evidence supports dependency and an animal depletion effect, not routine high-dose supplementation.'
    finding_statement: 'Pantothenate supports acetylcholine-synthesis capacity through coenzyme A and acetyl-CoA formation, and severe chronic pantothenate depletion can reduce brain acetylcholine synthesis in rats.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'In rats exposed chronically to ethanol, brain pantothenate fell to 7% of control and labelled acetylcholine synthesis from pyruvate was inhibited; pantothenate co-administration raised brain pantothenate and acetylcholine synthesis. Together with the established acetyl-CoA reaction requirement, this closes the pantothenate → coenzyme A/acetyl-CoA → synthesis chain.'
    synthesis_limitations: The intervention used chronic high-dose ethanol and pharmacological pantothenate doses in rats. It does not establish that ordinary B5 intake limits acetylcholine synthesis or that supplementation benefits adequately nourished humans.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Rivera-Calimlim et al. (1988)
        citation_key: rivera_calimlim_pantothenic_1988
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#rivera_calimlim_pantothenic_1988
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: isolated-substance
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Chronic ethanol depleted rat-brain pantothenate and inhibited acetylcholine synthesis, while pantothenate co-administration increased both brain pantothenate and synthesis.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Chronic and acute ethanol exposure with or without oral pantothenate in rats, measuring labelled acetylcholine synthesis.'
          population: Rats; no human participants.
          result: The chronic four-month condition reduced brain pantothenate and acetylcholine synthesis; pantothenate co-treatment partly restored both.
          effect_magnitude: Brain pantothenate fell to 7% of control with chronic ethanol; synthesis differences were statistically significant but no transferable human effect size is available.
          evidence_summary: Directly links severe pantothenate depletion to reduced acetylcholine synthesis through acetyl-CoA provision.
          limitations: 'Ethanol-specific animal model, very high pantothenate doses, and no ordinary-diet or human outcome.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F6
    finding_label: One-carbon insufficiency can constrain the choline resource used for acetylcholine
    finding_summary: Folate- and B12-dependent one-carbon metabolism shares choline-related methyl resources. Dietary or genetic impairment can lower brain choline and acetylcholine in animal models.
    finding_interpretation: 'This supports a constrained-by mapping to the Methyl Donor Pool. It does not make folate, B12, or betaine ChAT cofactors or separate Direct Dietary Requirements.'
    finding_statement: 'Inadequate folate-dependent or B12-dependent methionine-cycle capacity can disturb brain choline metabolism and lower acetylcholine availability, creating a supported shared-resource constraint on acetylcholine-synthesis capacity.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Dietary folate compromise lowered brain choline and acetylcholine in mice, with SAM restoring both under the deficient condition. Genetic methionine-synthase-reductase impairment likewise lowered hippocampal choline, betaine, and acetylcholine. A separate rat study found mixed, region- and age-dependent acetylcholine changes, showing that the effect is not uniform. Together these sources establish a shared-resource constraint while preserving biological variability.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Animal dietary and genetic models measure metabolite pools more often than synthesis flux. They do not show that folate, B12, betaine, or SAM supplementation raises acetylcholine synthesis in nutrient-replete humans.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Chan et al. (2008)
        citation_key: chan_folate_acetylcholine_2008
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#chan_folate_acetylcholine_2008
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Dietary folate compromise lowered mouse-brain choline and acetylcholine, while SAM supplementation under folate deficiency restored both pools.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Dietary folate deficiency across adult, aged, and genetically susceptible mouse models with SAM rescue.'
          population: Mice of several genotypes and ages.
          result: Folate compromise reduced choline and acetylcholine; SAM restored these measures and cognitive performance in the deficient condition.
          effect_magnitude: Directionally consistent rescue across several mouse contexts; no human effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Supports the link from one-carbon donor insufficiency to loss of the choline resource used for acetylcholine.
          limitations: 'Mixed dietary, oxidative, age, and genotype contexts; pool concentrations rather than direct synthesis flux.'
      - label: Jadavji et al. (2014)
        citation_key: jadavji_mtrr_choline_2014
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jadavji_mtrr_choline_2014
        data_level: Preclinical
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Methionine-synthase-reductase-deficient mice had lower hippocampal choline, betaine, and acetylcholine with compensatory ChAT and AChE expression changes.'
        assessment:
          study: Genetic mouse model of impaired methionine synthase reductase.
          population: Three-month-old wild-type and Mtrr-deficient mice.
          result: 'Deficiency reduced hippocampal choline, betaine, and acetylcholine and impaired short-term memory.'
          effect_magnitude: Significant group differences reported; no dietary or human effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Adds B12-dependent methionine-cycle evidence to the shared-resource constraint.
          limitations: Genetic mouse model; altered concentration and enzyme expression do not quantify synthesis flux.
      - label: Crivello et al. (2010)
        citation_key: crivello_folate_choline_2010
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#crivello_folate_choline_2010
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Ten weeks of folate deficiency changed brain acetylcholine in adult rats by region—lower in hippocampus but higher in cortex and striatum—with little brain effect in young rats.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled folate-deficient versus control diets in young and adult male rats.
          population: Male Sprague Dawley rats starting at four weeks or nine months.
          result: Brain choline and acetylcholine responses depended on age and region rather than moving uniformly.
          effect_magnitude: Significant regional differences; no whole-brain or human synthesis estimate.
          evidence_summary: Qualifies the constraint as context-dependent and prevents a universal lower-acetylcholine claim.
          limitations: Concentrations rather than synthesis flux; animal model; mixed regional direction.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F7
    finding_label: Acetyl-CoA supply is metabolically generated and compartmented
    finding_summary: 'Choline acetyltransferase works in the neuronal cytosol, while much acetyl-CoA is generated in mitochondria. Acetyl-unit transfer and local regeneration therefore form a separate substrate-supply control.'
    finding_interpretation: 'Acetyl-CoA availability can constrain synthesis, but this does not make glucose, pyruvate, citrate, or dietary acetyl-CoA separate Dietary Requirements for this PM.'
    finding_statement: 'Cytosolic acetyl-CoA for acetylcholine synthesis is supplied through compartmented neuronal metabolism, and its availability can regulate synthesis independently of choline transport.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A focused review of brain acetylcholine synthesis distinguishes mitochondrial acetyl-CoA production from the cytosolic ChAT reaction and reviews citrate cleavage, pyruvate-dependent production, and possible direct mitochondrial export routes. The evidence supports acetyl-CoA availability as a control point while leaving the proportional contribution of each route context-dependent.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The source literature is mechanistic and largely preclinical, and competing acetyl-unit transfer routes were not fully resolved. It does not establish glucose, pyruvate, citrate, or acetyl-CoA as useful dietary targets for this PM.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Jope (1979)
        citation_key: jope_choline_acetylcoa_1979
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jope_choline_acetylcoa_1979
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Acetyl-CoA availability may limit acetylcholine synthesis, with evidence for citrate-lyase, pyruvate-dehydrogenase, and mitochondrial export routes supplying the cytosolic reaction.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Review of high-affinity choline transport, acetyl-CoA production, compartmentation, and regulation of brain acetylcholine synthesis.'
          population: 'Biochemical, synaptosomal, and animal literature; no dietary human trial.'
          result: Distinguished mitochondrial acetyl-CoA generation from cytosolic use by ChAT and identified several supported supply routes.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled dietary or clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes compartmented acetyl-CoA provision as a second upstream substrate-control problem.
          limitations: Older mechanistic literature; the relative contribution of proposed routes remains context-dependent.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Szutowicz et al. (2010)
        citation_key: szutowicz_thiamine_acetylcoa_2010
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#szutowicz_thiamine_acetylcoa_2010
        data_level: Preclinical
        why_relevant: 'Pyrithiamine-induced thiamine deficiency reduced pyruvate-dehydrogenase flux and mitochondrial and cytosolic acetyl-CoA in rat nerve terminals, supporting the compartmented acetyl-unit supply model.'
        why_excluded: 'The reported cholinergic endpoint was altered quantal acetylcholine release, while ChAT activity was unchanged; it does not establish vitamin B1 as a PM6 synthesis requirement or intake-responsive lever.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM6-F3
    finding_label: Cholinergic biology is translationally relevant to attention
    finding_summary: 'Acetylcholine-receptor and choline-status findings sit near attention biology in ADHD-related samples. That is translational context, not an ADHD treatment rule.'
    finding_interpretation: Use these studies as attention-relevant cholinergic context. They do not show that choline supplementation treats ADHD.
    finding_statement: Human ADHD-related muscarinic-binding and choline-status evidence is translationally relevant to attention; it is not a demonstration that changing choline intake treats ADHD.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: Lower muscarinic binding in boys with ADHD and choline-status discussion in a neurodevelopmental review together support a cholinergic context for attention. They do not isolate acetylcholine synthesis as a treatment target and they do not measure attention after a choline intervention designed to change synthesis.
    synthesis_limitations: Cross-sectional receptor binding and a narrative review. No choline intervention arm for ADHD or attention scores is attached.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Johansson et al. (2013)
        citation_key: johansson_decreased_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#johansson_decreased_2013
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'Decreased muscarinic binding in boys with ADHD supplies attention-relevant cholinergic context, not a treatment effect.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Same fibroblast binding comparison used in PM6-F1, reused here for the attention relationship.'
          population: Boys with ADHD and comparison boys.
          result: Lower muscarinic binding in the ADHD group.
          effect_magnitude: Binding contrast only; no attention-score change after diet.

### Overview

Acetylcholine is made in nerve endings when choline is joined to acetyl-CoA, a cell-made acetate carrier. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Diet can provide choline itself or choline from phosphatidylcholine, and vitamin B5 supports the acetyl-CoA side. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Entry into the nerve ending still controls access to the reaction. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) The reaction supplies acetylcholine for later cholinergic signalling. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

- **Benefits:** Acetylcholine is the transmitter cholinergic circuits use for attention and learning. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) That biological role is not a shown gain in attention from more choline. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
- **Implementation Notes:** Choline, phosphatidylcholine, and vitamin B5 are the provision routes. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Acetyl-CoA is made inside the cell and is not a dietary target. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) No dose is established for raising brain acetylcholine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Cholinergic signalling depends on a nerve terminal having both reaction substrates at the right place and time. Choline must first enter through a high-affinity transporter; choline acetyltransferase then transfers an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA. This synthesis capacity is different from the amount of acetylcholine stored, released, or detected at receptors.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Substrate transport and acetylcholine synthesis — mechanistic detail</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Choline entry is a regulated supply step)

Choline reaching the brain and choline entering a cholinergic nerve terminal are separate steps. CTL1/CTL2 transport systems operate at brain microvascular endothelium, whereas the high-affinity transporter CHT/SLC5A7 recovers choline into cholinergic nerve terminals. CHT activity and movement to the cell surface respond to neuronal activity, making terminal transport a major control point rather than a passive reflection of how much choline was eaten. Ojiakor and Rylett (2020) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) review terminal transport; Inazu (2019) [[13]](#pm-ref-13) reviews the blood–brain boundary.

#### (Two substrates form acetylcholine)

Inside the terminal, choline acetyltransferase transfers the acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to choline, forming acetylcholine and coenzyme A. Choline and acetyl-CoA are therefore reaction substrates; the enzyme does not use folate, vitamin B12, or pantothenate directly as cofactors. Oda (1999) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) establishes the enzyme chemistry.

#### (Acetyl-CoA has its own compartmented supply route)

ChAT uses acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, but much neuronal acetyl-CoA is generated in mitochondria. Acetyl units can reach the cytosolic pool through routes including citrate export and ATP-citrate-lyase cleavage, alongside other proposed pyruvate-dependent or mitochondrial-export routes. Their relative contribution is not fully settled, but acetyl-CoA availability can regulate synthesis independently of choline transport. Jope (1979) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) reviews this evidence. It does not make glucose, pyruvate, citrate, or dietary acetyl-CoA separate requirements on this page.

#### (Dietary provision reaches the two substrates by different routes)

Phosphatidylcholine is a choline-containing dietary form. Human tracer evidence shows that it is digested and remodelled, with labelled choline appearing in plasma; it is therefore a provision route to choline, not another ChAT substrate. Böckmann et al. (2023) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) measured this route. Pantothenate supports the other side of the reaction by supplying coenzyme A for acetyl-CoA formation. Severe pantothenate depletion reduced labelled brain acetylcholine synthesis in a chronic rat model, and pantothenate co-administration increased it. Rivera-Calimlim et al. (1988) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) do not establish a routine human supplementation effect.

#### (A shared one-carbon resource can change choline availability)

Choline can also be oxidised to betaine for one-carbon metabolism (the network that transfers methyl groups). Folate compromise and genetic impairment of B12-dependent methionine-cycle function lowered brain choline and acetylcholine in animal models, although regional responses were not uniform. Chan et al. (2008) [[9]](#pm-ref-9), Crivello et al. (2010) [[10]](#pm-ref-10), and Jadavji et al. (2014) [[11]](#pm-ref-11) support a shared-resource constraint, not a claim that folate, B12, or betaine run the ChAT reaction.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Synthesis ends when acetylcholine has been formed. Packaging by the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, release into the synapse, receptor binding, breakdown by acetylcholinesterase, and the resulting cognitive effects are later stages. Acetylcholine concentration also reflects storage, release, and breakdown, so concentration alone is not a synthesis-rate measurement.

#### (Integration within BRS1)

This synthesis capacity supports [BRS1(FM2) — Cholinergic Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-cholinergic-function). Choline allocation also intersects BRS2 remethylation and phosphatidylcholine biology, while the [BRS2(KC1) — Methyl Donor Pool](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/kc/brs2-kc1-one-carbon-donor-pool) can constrain how much choline remains available for the synthesis substrate pool.

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Transporter evidence identifies terminal choline uptake as a control step for acetylcholine synthesis, while human tracing demonstrates systemic assimilation of choline from dietary phosphatidylcholine. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Animal depletion and rescue studies support bounded pantothenate and one-carbon dependencies, with acetylcholine responses varying by experimental condition, region and age. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) The evidence therefore supports provision and local synthesis capacity without equating plasma choline delivery with neuronal release, attention benefit or a human dose response.

## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections

### 5.1 BRS Pathways

- None listed

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) — Folate- and B12-dependent remethylation provides an alternative to choline-derived betaine for methyl donation. When this route is impaired, animal evidence shows lower brain choline and acetylcholine, creating a downstream substrate constraint here.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation) — Oxidation of choline supplies betaine to this remethylation route. That competing use links methyl-donor demand to choline availability, but dietary betaine has not been shown here to increase human brain acetylcholine synthesis.
- [BRS2-FM3-PM7 — Phosphatidylcholine Formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation) — Phosphatidylcholine is a major choline-containing membrane and dietary form. Its digestion can provide circulating choline, while its synthesis and membrane roles remain distinct from the ChAT reaction.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.
