scientific_findings_intro: >-
  Butyrate and zinc experiments directly interrogate epithelial junction function. Retinoids influence
  differentiation and permeability, but their direction depends on the model. A selected postinfectious IBS
  trial found a glutamine response; heterogeneous supplementation evidence does not support a general regimen.
  Microbiota associations do not establish a barrier-to-cognition effect. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
  [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Alcohol studies identify a context-specific barrier
  stressor and recovery relationship; carotenoid absorption supports upstream delivery, and fermented-milk
  findings remain preparation- and population-specific.
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM1-F1
    finding_label: Tight junctions govern selective paracellular permeability
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: false
    finding_summary: >-
      Intestinal epithelial tight junctions form regulated pore and leak pathways that determine selective
      paracellular passage.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This supports the PM boundary around epithelial gate function. Downstream microbial-product containment
      and systemic inflammation remain outside it.
    finding_statement: >-
      Intestinal tight-junction structure and regulation determine selective paracellular permeability, while
      epithelial injury can create a distinct unrestricted permeability pathway.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      An authoritative mechanistic review distinguishes tight-junction-dependent pore and leak pathways from
      unrestricted flux caused by epithelial damage. In a mouse pneumonia model, increased permeability and
      claudin-2 were attenuated by oral LGG, providing intervention evidence that barrier permeability and
      junction-associated biology can move together under pathological conditions.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The review establishes mechanism rather than dietary responsiveness. The LGG experiment was performed in
      young mice with experimental Pseudomonas pneumonia, not in healthy humans, and does not establish a
      generic fermented-food effect.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Chanez-Paredes and Turner (2023)
        citation_key: chanez_paredes_paracellular_2023
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#chanez_paredes_paracellular_2023
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Tight junctions define size- and charge-selective pore and leak pathways; epithelial damage produces
          a separate unrestricted pathway.
      - label: Khailova et al. (2017)
        citation_key: khailova_lactobacillus_2017
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#khailova_lactobacillus_2017
        data_level: Animal Data
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Oral LGG attenuated pneumonia-induced intestinal permeability and claudin-2 elevation and supported
          mucin expression in mice.
  - id: PM1-F2
    finding_label: Butyrate can support epithelial tight-junction assembly
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: false
    finding_summary: Microbial fermentation products, especially butyrate, can act directly on epithelial barrier biology.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This supports a Direct butyrate relationship and a Derived fermentable-fibre provision relationship,
      with microbiota and fibre-specific limitations.
    finding_statement: >-
      Butyrate can function as an epithelial metabolic substrate and promote intestinal tight-junction
      assembly, while fermentable dietary fibre lies upstream as microbial substrate provision for
      short-chain-fatty-acid production.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      In Caco-2 monolayers, physiological butyrate increased transepithelial resistance, reduced inulin
      permeability and accelerated tight-junction assembly alongside AMPK activation. A broader review links
      microbial fermentation of dietary substrates to short-chain-fatty-acid production and intestinal barrier
      effects.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The direct assembly experiment is an immortalised epithelial-cell model. Fibre-to-butyrate conversion
      varies by fibre structure and microbial ecology, and neither source establishes a universal human intake
      threshold, a generic effect of all fibre, or oral butyrate as necessary treatment.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Peng et al. (2009)
        citation_key: peng_butyrate_2009
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#peng_butyrate_2009
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Butyrate increased barrier resistance, reduced inulin permeability and accelerated tight-junction
          assembly in Caco-2 monolayers.
      - label: Silva et al. (2020)
        citation_key: silva_role_2020
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#silva_role_2020
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          The review links microbial fermentation-derived short-chain fatty acids with epithelial barrier and
          gut-brain communication mechanisms.
  - id: PM1-F3
    finding_label: Barrier markers and attention-related symptoms are associated, not causal
    presentation: phenome-relationship
    primary_phenome: Focus / Attention Stability
    finding_summary: >-
      One small cross-sectional ADHD study linked serum zonulin with hyperactivity, but it did not establish a
      causal tight-junction-to-attention pathway.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      The evidence is compatible with the proposed relationship but is too indirect to show that changing PM1
      changes attention stability.
    finding_statement: >-
      Current human evidence provides only indirect observational support for a relationship between
      intestinal barrier biology and attention-related symptoms.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      In children with ADHD, serum zonulin was independently associated with hyperactivity and social-function
      scores. A separate microbiota study found lower Faecalibacterium abundance associated with parent-rated
      ADHD symptoms, but it did not measure barrier function. Together these studies support hypothesis
      generation, not a PM1-specific causal relationship.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Both studies are small and cross-sectional. Serum zonulin is an indirect permeability marker; neither
      study manipulated or directly quantified tight-junction integrity, and neither demonstrates that PM1
      changes attention outcomes.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Özyurt et al. (2018)
        citation_key: ozyurt_increased_2018
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ozyurt_increased_2018
        data_level: Human Study
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Higher serum zonulin was independently associated with greater hyperactivity and social impairment
          in children with ADHD.
      - label: Jiang et al. (2018)
        citation_key: jiang_gut_2018
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jiang_gut_2018
        data_level: Human Study
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Lower Faecalibacterium abundance was associated with parent-rated ADHD symptoms, but permeability
          and tight-junction function were not measured.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        The two studies address different proxies and cannot be treated as independent replications of a PM1 →
        attention relationship.
    fm_rollup: false
  - id: PM1-F4
    finding_label: Direct evidence for an Emotional Regulation relationship is absent
    presentation: phenome-relationship
    primary_phenome: Emotional Regulation
    finding_summary: The attached human study does not measure PM1 or emotional regulation.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Emotional Regulation remains a framework-level hypothesis rather than an evidence-established PM1
      relationship.
    finding_statement: >-
      The bounded evidence assessment does not establish that gut tight-junction integrity modulates Emotional
      Regulation.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Jiang et al. measured faecal microbiota composition and parent-rated ADHD symptoms. It did not measure
      intestinal permeability, tight-junction function or emotional-regulation outcomes, so it cannot directly
      support the current PM1 → Emotional Regulation proposition.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      This is an evidence-gap adjudication, not evidence that no biological relationship exists. Targeted
      barrier measures and emotional-regulation outcomes would be needed to test the proposition.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Jiang et al. (2018)
        citation_key: jiang_gut_2018
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#jiang_gut_2018
        data_level: Human Study
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          The study reported microbiota-composition associations with ADHD symptoms but did not measure either
          PM1 or emotional regulation.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Jiang et al. is also assessed in PM1-F3 because the same attached study was previously used for both
        Phenome relationships; that reuse is not independent evidence.
    fm_rollup: false
  - id: PM1-F5
    finding_label: Retinoid and zinc effects depend on the epithelial context
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: false
    finding_summary: >-
      Cellular zinc supports junction-protein maintenance; retinoic acid influences epithelial differentiation
      and selective permeability.
    finding_statement: >-
      Cellular zinc supports junction-protein maintenance; retinoic acid influences epithelial differentiation
      and selective permeability.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      The zinc result supports a bounded cellular requirement. Retinoid biology cannot be simplified to lower
      permeability in every context.
    synthesis: >-
      The zinc result supports a bounded cellular requirement. Retinoid biology cannot be simplified to lower
      permeability in every context.
    synthesis_limitations: Cell experiments and mechanistic synthesis do not define dietary thresholds or extra-intake benefit.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored

      resistant-starch substrate reaches a capable microbial community; (2) utilisation and cross-feeding
      generate a context-dependent butyrate pool; (3) luminal butyrate becomes available to and is taken up by

## BRS5-1-1 - Gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity


## 1. Mission & Overview

### Mission

Maintain epithelial tight junction integrity and selective permeability at the gut lining.

**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Supported. Dietary inputs are the principal group displayed here, within the study-specific boundaries. Comparative dominance is not established.

### Overview

The gut lining is a selective gate. Tight junctions, the seals between its cells, control which materials pass between them. Maintaining that selectivity helps protect the body while allowing normal exchange. Butyrate, cellular zinc and retinoid signalling affect epithelial functions in experimental models; glutamine has a condition-specific human permeability result. These findings identify different biological routes rather than a universal gut-repair supplement. [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

- **Benefits:** Selective permeability helps limit inappropriate passage across the gut lining; symptom benefits from supplementation are specific to the populations studied.
- **Implementation Notes:** Fermentable substrates can supply microbial butyrate. Nutrient adequacy differs from extra-intake benefit; the glutamine trial concerned postinfectious diarrhoea-predominant IBS with confirmed hyperpermeability.
- **Biological Relevance:** This PM concerns epithelial junction regulation. Mucus-specific microbial effects belong to PM3 and bioactive endotoxin containment to PM2. Lower electrical resistance may reflect selective ion permeability rather than unrestricted leakage.

## 2. Primary Biological Effects

↑ tight-junction strength; ↓ permeability

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Cellular zinc supports junction-protein maintenance; retinoic acid influences epithelial differentiation and selective permeability. [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

#### Biological process

The zinc result supports a bounded cellular requirement. Retinoid biology cannot be simplified to lower permeability in every context. [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

#### Mechanism Boundary

This PM concerns epithelial junction regulation. Mucus-specific microbial effects belong to PM3 and bioactive endotoxin containment to PM2. Lower electrical resistance may reflect selective ion permeability rather than unrestricted leakage.

#### Integration

This PM contributes its specific process to its parent FM. Shared inputs do not merge distinct jobs or prove an integrated clinical outcome.

    presentation: mechanistic-basis

(Neurotransmitter Protein Requirements)

## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers

**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Dominant

### Overview

Food protein supplies indispensable amino acids—the amino acids the body cannot make in sufficient amounts—including phenylalanine and tryptophan. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Phenylalanine can also be converted to tyrosine. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) After a protein meal, dietary phenylalanine appears in the circulation. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Tyrosine and tryptophan are precursors later signalling can use for dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Protein that covers those amino acids is the supported dietary route. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

- **Benefits:** These amino acids, including tyrosine made from phenylalanine, are how meal protein supplies the pool that dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin pathways draw on. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) That capacity is not evidence that extra protein improves attention or mood. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[6]](#pm-ref-6)
- **Implementation Notes:** Indispensable amino-acid supply and tryptophan are the dietary requirements; food protein supplies these amino acids. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Tyrosine is made from phenylalanine, so it is not classed as an indispensable amino acid. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) No neurotransmitter-targeted intake dose is established. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Each meal does not have to supply the full set. [[5]](#pm-ref-5)
- **Biological Relevance:** Those amino acids still have to cross into the brain before they are used to make dopamine, noradrenaline or serotonin - see [PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation).

## 2. Primary Biological Effects
↑ circulating indispensable amino-acid supply, including phenylalanine that can be converted to tyrosine

## 4. Mechanistic Basis + Scientific Findings (SFs 6)

Phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase (PAH) contributes to endogenous tyrosine supply. The established reaction is documented in [Scientific Principles](?review=1#pm1-sp1). [UniProt C1](#pm-curated-pah) and [Rhea C2](#pm-curated-rhea) establish reaction identity, not an independent dietary cofactor admission.


### Summary

The six Findings distinguish [dietary delivery](#pm1-mechanism-f1), [whole-diet adequacy](#pm1-mechanism-f2), [endogenous tyrosine supply](#pm1-mechanism-f3), [food texture](#pm1-mechanism-f5), [extrusion kinetics](#pm1-mechanism-f6) and [oral tyrosine](#pm1-mechanism-f7). Later signalling can use tyrosine and tryptophan only after those amino acids are available in the circulation. A protein meal is what puts dietary phenylalanine there, and phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine. Brain entry and neurotransmitter synthesis come after that. [Oral tyrosine supply](#pm1-mechanism-f7) has also been measured as a circulating concentration response, not as brain delivery.

Dietary tracer appearance identifies amino acids arriving from the ingested food. Total plasma concentration also reflects endogenous turnover, tissue uptake and clearance. A higher tracer appearance or earlier peak is therefore not automatically a larger usable brain precursor supply, and neither establishes attention or mood benefit. <span id="pm1-mechanism-f1" />

<span id="circulating-supply" />

#### PM1-F1

Gorissen et al. (2020) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) pooled human trials of labelled whey, casein and milk protein. About half of the dietary phenylalanine appeared in the circulation over five hours. Casein delivered a smaller fraction than whey or milk, a larger dose delivered more, and the older subgroup showed a lower fraction appearing within the measurement window. That pooled association does not establish uniform age-related impairment. The measured endpoint is plasma phenylalanine, not brain dopamine, noradrenaline or serotonin.

Supporting evidence: [PM1-F1](#pm1-f1).

<span id="pm1-mechanism-f2" />

<span id="coverage-across-the-diet" />

#### PM1-F2

Mariotti and Gardner (2019) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) found that adult vegetarian diets which include protein-rich plant foods can meet protein and amino-acid requirements. Moughan and Lim (2024) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) score protein quality by digestible indispensable amino acids, not by grams alone. Marsh et al. (2013) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) state that varied plant proteins across the diet can cover that set, so complementary proteins do not have to share every meal.

Supporting evidence: [PM1-F2](#pm1-f2).

<span id="pm1-mechanism-f3" />

<span id="phenylalanine-tyrosine-and-tryptophan" />

#### PM1-F3

Human tracer studies demonstrate phenylalanine conversion to tyrosine and regional contributions to circulating supply, including renal conversion and net release in the fasted setting. [[26]](#pm-ref-26) [[27]](#pm-ref-27) Matthews (2007) supplies kinetic context. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) Intracellular precursor enrichment limits quantitative organ attribution; no dietary dose or brain effect is established. The curated PAH records establish reaction identity separately. [UniProt C1](#pm-curated-pah); [Rhea C2](#pm-curated-rhea).

Supporting evidence: [PM1-F3](#pm1-f3). Established reaction identity: [Scientific Principle — Phenylalanine hydroxylase reaction](?review=1#pm1-sp1).

<span id="pm1-mechanism-f4" />

#### PM1-F4

Aquili (2020) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) names tryptophan as the serotonin precursor and tyrosine as the dopamine precursor. Those names identify the amino acids in this pool. They do not show that a higher circulating supply raises brain serotonin or dopamine. Brain transport and downstream synthesis remain distinct from circulating provision.

Foundational provenance: [Scientific Principle — Tyrosine and tryptophan precursor identities](?review=1#pm1-sp2). Historical record: [PM1-F4](?review=1#pm1-f4).

<span id="pm1-mechanism-f5" />

#### PM1-F5

Food structure can modify the time course and measured appearance of amino acids from an ingested protein source. In the matched beef-texture experiment, more dietary phenylalanine appeared in the circulation after mincing, but total plasma essential-amino-acid concentrations and muscle protein synthesis did not differ detectably. Dietary tracer appearance and total circulating concentration are different measurements; neither establishes greater brain precursor delivery. [Pennings et al.](#stage2-ref-pm1-pennings2013).

Supporting evidence: [PM1-F5](#pm1-f5). The preparation-specific SOP is admitted for the tested older-male meal, without a brain-delivery or clinical-benefit claim.

<span id="pm1-mechanism-f6" />

#### PM1-F6

Processing can alter the temporal response without demonstrating a change in total measured exposure. The tested extruded mycoprotein/pea blend changed selected early plasma amino-acid responses, while the integrated five-hour grouped responses were not significantly different. Unlike the beef experiment, this study did not use a dietary tracer; the endpoints must not be treated as interchangeable or as proof of equal absorption. [Extrusion crossover](#stage2-ref-pm1-extrusion2024).

Supporting evidence: [PM1-F6](#pm1-f6). No extrusion-related SOP is admitted.

<span id="pm1-mechanism-f7" />

#### PM1-F7

In eleven subjects, plasma tyrosine increased during a protein-containing dietary day and rose further with divided oral L-tyrosine. This supports provision to the circulating precursor pool. Plasma concentration does not measure dietary appearance flux, brain entry or catecholamine synthesis, and the small meal/supplement experiment does not establish a general food-effective dose or benefit from additional intake. [[23]](#pm-ref-23)

Supporting evidence: [PM1-F7](#pm1-f7).

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Competitive transport of amino acids across the blood–brain barrier is [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation). Dopamine synthesis and signalling are [BRS1-FM1-PM3 — Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation). Noradrenaline signalling is [BRS1-FM1-PM4 — Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation). Serotonin signalling is [BRS1-FM1-PM5 — Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation).

#### (Integration within BRS1)

This mechanism supplies the circulating pool at the start of [BRS1(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function). Later mechanisms in that pathway draw on it. A shared key-constraint mapping is not established.

</div>
</div>
</div>



### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Dietary protein supplies the circulating precursor pool; food structure and source can alter delivery kinetics without proving superior neurotransmitter function. Curated reaction identity, whole-diet adequacy and experimental intervention findings are distinguished below.

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency) — Methylation uses methionine, another indispensable amino acid supplied by dietary protein. That is a shared amino-acid source, not a control this mechanism exerts on the methylation cycle.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS1-FM1-PM2 - LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) — The tyrosine and tryptophan in this circulating pool still have to enter the brain. That entry is competitive transport, not this supply step.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM3 - Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) — Dopamine synthesis uses tyrosine after brain entry, including tyrosine made from phenylalanine. This mechanism supplies that precursor. It does not carry out the synthesis.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM4 - Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) — Noradrenaline synthesis uses the same tyrosine after brain entry. This mechanism supplies the circulating precursor and does not regulate noradrenaline signalling.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM5 - Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation) — Serotonin synthesis uses tryptophan from this pool. This mechanism supplies that indispensable amino acid and does not carry out serotonin synthesis.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

    title: Additional upstream nutrients are not automatically recycling interventions
    citation_keys:

    finding_ids:

    establishes: >-

      independently assessed dietary precursor relationship to FAD.
    cannot_establish: >-
      That dietary niacin, glucose, cysteine, glycine or oral glutathione independently controls this
      recycling operation merely because it contributes to an upstream metabolite or synthesis pathway.
    missing_link: >-
      Each additional proposed input needs evidence connecting its dietary supply to this specific
      regeneration operation; glutathione synthesis and glutathione recycling are different steps.
    required_evidence: >-
      Input-specific dietary supply and enzyme-capacity evidence, or mechanism-engagement evidence for the
      exact receiving operation, retaining compartment and nutritional-status limitations.
    affected_relationship: Candidate NADPH and glutathione supply routes; no new dietary admission for these inputs.

  Regenerate vitamin and thiol antioxidants across networked systems so endogenous defence capacity is
  sustained.

scientific_findings:
  - id: PM6-F1
    finding_label: Vitamin C reduces the vitamin E radical
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Pulse radiolysis showed vitamin C reacting with the vitamin E radical. The interaction can return
      vitamin E toward its working form. Kinetic reviews describe the same partnership as extending vitamin E
      capacity. This is not an intake trial.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This is the recycling job. It is different from vitamin E stopping peroxyl radicals in the membrane, and
      it is not a reason to take high doses.
    finding_statement: >-
      Vitamin C can reduce the vitamin E radical. That regeneration is a biochemical partnership. It does not
      set a high-dose intake.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Packer, Slater and Willson observed a free-radical interaction between vitamin E and vitamin C by pulse
      radiolysis: ascorbate reduced the tocopheroxyl radical. Niki states that the synergistic interaction of
      vitamin E and vitamin C enhances the antioxidant capacity of vitamin E. Neither source is a feeding
      trial.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The observation is chemical. It does not show that eating more vitamin C or vitamin E speeds recycling
      in people.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Packer, Slater and Willson (1979)
        citation_key: packer_direct_1979
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#packer_direct_1979
        data_level: Mechanistic
        exposure_context: pulse radiolysis of vitamin E and vitamin C radicals
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search

## BRS3-2-6 - Antioxidant Network Recycling

(Recycling the Body's Antioxidant Defences)

## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers

### Mission

Regenerate vitamin and thiol antioxidants across networked systems so endogenous defence capacity is sustained.


**Intervention Dominance:** Not established — No principal intervention route established

Ascorbate reduces the vitamin E radical in a chemical observation. No cited study shows that raising vitamin C or vitamin E intake speeds that recycling.

### Overview

Vitamin C can reduce the vitamin E radical and return vitamin E toward its working form. Packer, Slater and Willson (1979) observed that reaction directly. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Niki (2014) describes the same partnership as extending vitamin E capacity. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) This is regeneration, not the chain-breaking job vitamin E does in membranes, and it is not a high-dose rule.

- **Benefits:** Regenerating vitamin E after it has acted lets that antioxidant keep working longer than one reaction. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)
- **Implementation Notes:** Vitamin C and vitamin E are the nutrients in this reaction. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) No intake was shown to speed it. Extra vitamin E is not a benefit. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)
- **Biological Relevance:** Defence-gene regulation is a different step — see PM3. Vitamin E breaking peroxyl-radical chains in membranes is a different job — see PM5.

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Antioxidant protection persists only when depleted antioxidants are regenerated across interacting systems. Network recycling—not isolated nutrient presence—determines whether redox defence remains effective within [BRS3(FM2) - Antioxidant Defense Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity).

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Antioxidant-network logic and recycling capacity</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Network rather than single-nutrient protection)

Packer, Slater and Willson (1979) observed ascorbate reducing the vitamin E radical. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Niki (2014) describes that partnership as extending vitamin E capacity. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Glutathione and other thiols are sometimes placed in a wider network. They are not a dietary glutathione target here — see PM4.

Riboflavin supplies the precursor of the FAD cofactor used by glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione. Human red-cell enzyme responses support this supply relationship; they do not measure neuronal recycling or justify extra intake above adequacy. [[11]](#pm-ref-11)

#### (Regeneration cycles and cofactor dependence)

The recycling job is vitamin C reducing the vitamin E radical. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Vitamin E stopping peroxyl radicals in the membrane is a different job — see PM5. Klein et al. (2011) found more prostate cancers with 400 IU of vitamin E a day, so this chemistry is not a high-dose rule. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Transcriptional Nrf2 induction belongs to [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation). Net ROS generation versus clearance is handled by [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance). Membrane lipid peroxidation control is represented by [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control).

#### (Integration within BRS3)

This PM encodes regeneration of vitamin E by vitamin C within [BRS3(FM2)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity). No shared-pool mapping is established. Mitochondrial electron transport can change how fast radicals are formed, which is a neighbouring pressure on this recycling step, not the recycling reaction itself — see [BRS4-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function).

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS4-FM1-PM1 — Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) — Electron transport is a source of the oxidative load this network regenerates against. It is not the vitamin-to-vitamin recycling step.
- [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) — Mitochondrial reactive-oxygen control is upstream oxidative pressure. This page regenerates spent antioxidants and does not set that production rate.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) — Nrf2 regulates defence-gene expression. It does not return oxidised vitamin E to its working form.
- [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) — Clearance balance is the net oxidative pressure. Recycling keeps the antioxidant network available for that clearance.
- [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — Lipid peroxidation is the membrane-fat damage that vitamin E interrupts. Recycling restores that vitamin after it has been used.

scientific_findings_intro: 'Human PET and plasma measurements estimated whole-brain DHA incorporation at 3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day; turnover and half-life estimates additionally used a previously reported brain DHA pool and steady-state assumptions. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) A porcine study found greater gray-matter DHA accretion from phospholipid-bound than triglyceride-bound DHA, consistent with reviewed carrier-dependent delivery biology. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) These findings establish measured incorporation and delivery-form relevance, without defining an optimal oral dose, capsule-to-brain transfer fraction or cognitive benefit.'
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM7-F1
    finding_label: DHA is a structural neuronal-membrane polyunsaturated fat
    finding_summary: 'Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) is a long-chain omega-3 fat built into neuronal-membrane phospholipids. That is a structural role, not a dosing rule.'
    finding_interpretation: This supports the mission of a signal-ready lipid foundation. It does not show that a single meal resets membranes or that DHA treats ADHD.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: DHA is a structural polyunsaturated fatty acid of neuronal membranes; that structural role is not a human dosing or ADHD-treatment rule.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: A review of omega-3 fats in brain development and function treats DHA as a major structural component of neuronal membranes with implications for signalling architecture. That supports reading this mechanism as membrane composition. It does not measure everyday dietary control of human membrane DHA or isolate ADHD treatment.
    synthesis_limitations: Narrative review spanning development and psychopathology hypotheses. It is not a human membrane-accretion trial after a defined DHA food form.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: McNamara and Carlson (2006)
        citation_key: mcnamara_role_2006
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#mcnamara_role_2006
        data_level: Animal Data
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'Long-chain omega-3 fats, especially DHA, are structural components of neuronal membranes relevant to brain development and function.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Narrative review of omega-3 roles in brain development, function and psychopathology risk.'
          population: 'Mixed developmental, animal and human literature summarised in the review.'
          result: Identified DHA as a principal membrane PUFA with signalling-architecture implications.
          effect_magnitude: No dietary dose-response or ADHD treatment estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the structural membrane role of DHA.
          limitations: Review synthesis; not a human incorporation trial.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM7-F2
    finding_label: LPC-DHA uses MFSD2A for barrier transport
    finding_summary: DHA carried as lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC-DHA) is a preferred substrate for MFSD2A transport at the blood–brain barrier. The phospholipid carrier form matters for presentation.
    finding_interpretation: Phospholipid-bound DHA is delivery context for this mechanism. It is not a second independent clinical lever and does not by itself prove that choline intake constrains incorporation.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: 'LPC-DHA is transported by MFSD2A more efficiently than free or triglyceride-bound DHA; carrier form is a transport property, not a choline-intake or ADHD-dosing rule.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: A phosphatidylcholine-DHA review describes conversion toward LPC-DHA and MFSD2A-mediated barrier transport as the efficient route relative to free or triglyceride-bound DHA. That establishes why phospholipid carriage is mechanistically distinct. It does not measure human membrane DHA after ordinary choline intake.
    synthesis_limitations: 'Mechanistic and disease-context review, including APOE4 discussion. It is not a human dietary-choline or ADHD trial.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Patrick (2019)
        citation_key: patrick_role_2019
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#patrick_role_2019
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'Phosphatidylcholine-DHA can generate LPC-DHA, which crosses the blood–brain barrier via MFSD2A more efficiently than non-phospholipid forms.'
        assessment:
          study: Review of phosphatidylcholine-DHA transport and APOE4-associated Alzheimer context.
          population: Mixed human genetic and mechanistic literature; not a dietary ADHD sample.
          result: Identified LPC-DHA / MFSD2A as the efficient barrier-transport route.
          effect_magnitude: No ordinary-diet incorporation estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes carrier-form transport chemistry.
          limitations: Review; does not show choline intake constrains DHA incorporation.
      - label: Quek et al. (2016)
        citation_key: quek_mfsd2a_transport_2016
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#quek_mfsd2a_transport_2016
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        exposure_context: Radiolabelled LPC and controlled transport-site/ion conditions.
        directional_finding: MFSD2A transport is sodium-dependent; human transporter binding-site mutations and lipid-uptake assays support the coupling mechanism.
        assessment:
          study: Human MFSD2A modelling with biochemical site-mutant lipid transport assays.
          population: Experimental cells expressing human transporter.
          result: MFSD2A transport is sodium-dependent; human transporter binding-site mutations and lipid-uptake assays support the coupling mechanism.
          effect_magnitude: No additional magnitude inferred.
          evidence_summary: MFSD2A transport is sodium-dependent; human transporter binding-site mutations and lipid-uptake assays support the coupling mechanism.
          limitations: 'This supports the specific LPC-DHA carrier route, not all DHA delivery or direct neural incorporation from a meal. Sodium homeostasis, carrier formation and membrane gradients intervene; no added-salt recommendation, food-effective dose or clinical benefit.'
          retrieval_scope: Primary transport/mutant experiments and model limitations retrieved 26 October 2026.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM7-F3
    finding_label: Phospholipid DHA accretes more than triglyceride DHA in a porcine model
    finding_summary: 'Dietary DHA provided as phospholipid produced higher gray-matter DHA accretion than the same fatty acid as triglyceride in neonatal piglets. That is an animal delivery-form finding, not a human dosing rule.'
    finding_interpretation: Use this as evidence that phospholipid versus triglyceride form can change accretion in that model. Do not read it as a human capsule dose or an ADHD protocol.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: Phospholipid-bound dietary DHA produced greater gray-matter DHA accretion than triglyceride-bound DHA in neonatal piglets; that animal contrast is not a human dosing or ADHD-treatment rule.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A controlled porcine comparison found about 1.9-fold greater gray-matter DHA accretion from phospholipid DHA than from triglyceride DHA. That supports a delivery-form difference for accretion. It does not establish human membrane dosing or that choline intake, rather than the DHA phospholipid itself, was the limiting input.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Neonatal piglets, not children or adults. The contrast is lipid class of DHA, not a choline-supplement arm.'

  - id: PM7-F5
    finding_label: Human brain DHA incorporation is not an oral dose requirement
    finding_summary: 'A PET study in 14 healthy adults estimated whole-brain DHA incorporation at 3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day. This is brain uptake from circulating unesterified DHA, not a dietary or supplement dose.'
    finding_interpretation: Distinguish measured tracer uptake and plasma DHA from model-derived net incorporation and turnover. These figures do not establish supplement efficacy or an optimal intake.
    fm_rollup: false
    finding_statement: Human PET estimates of circulating DHA incorporation quantify brain replacement under studied conditions; they do not directly measure oral dose requirements.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Umhau et al. combined intravenous [1-11C]DHA PET incorporation coefficients with plasma unesterified DHA concentrations to estimate 3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day (mean ± SD) for the whole brain. Using a previously reported 5 g brain DHA pool, the authors estimated approximately 0.076% daily turnover and a 911-day (about 2.5-year) half-life under a steady-state replacement model.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The 5 g pool was an external estimate, not measured brain DHA in these participants. Net consumption and half-life are model-derived. The study did not test oral dosing, distinguish all delivery routes, measure supplement benefit, or establish needs during development, deficiency or disease.'

          result: Measured tracer uptake and plasma DHA were used to calculate whole-brain net incorporation.
          effect_magnitude: 3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day; estimated 911-day half-life using a reported 5 g pool.
          evidence_summary: Quantifies adult brain incorporation rather than oral intake.
          limitations: Steady-state kinetic model; pool size assumed from prior literature; no oral supplementation comparison.

(Getting Omega-3 DHA Into Brain Membranes)

**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Dominant

### Overview

DHA, a long-chain omega-3 fat, is built into the phospholipids of neuronal membranes. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Membranes that contain it support the structure neurons use to signal. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) The carrier matters: DHA bound as lysophosphatidylcholine can cross into the brain, and in animals phospholipid DHA accumulated in the brain more than triglyceride DHA. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) That is structural delivery, not a general omega-3 effect. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

- **Benefits:** DHA in these membranes supports the fluidity and receptor movement that synaptic signalling depends on. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)
- **Implementation Notes:** DHA is the provision route. Phospholipid-bound DHA is a delivery form, not a second treatment, and the animal comparison does not set a human dose. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[5]](#pm-ref-5)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects
↑ brain DHA accretion; ↑ neuronal membrane DHA enrichment; ↑ membrane fluidity context; ↑ synaptic signalling competence

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Synaptic signalling depends partly on the lipid composition of neuronal membranes. Phosphatidylcholine can carry DHA; conversion toward lysophosphatidylcholine-DHA (LPC-DHA) presents DHA to the MFSD2A transporter at the blood–brain barrier. Delivery form, not dose slogans, is the mechanistic distinction. This is not an ADHD treatment claim.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>PC carriage, LPC-DHA transport, membrane incorporation, and synaptic signalling</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Phosphatidylcholine as DHA and EPA carrier)

Phosphatidylcholine is a principal membrane phospholipid and a dietary carrier for long-chain omega-3 fatty acids. DHA in that phospholipid pool supplies neuronal-membrane architecture and the chemistry that can generate LPC carriers → [Patrick, 2019]

#### (LPC-DHA and MFSD2A blood–brain barrier transport)

DHA in phosphatidylcholine can be converted to LPC-DHA, which crosses the blood–brain barrier more efficiently than free DHA or triglyceride-bound forms via MFSD2A. That transport step precedes structural incorporation and explains why phospholipid-matrix delivery is distinct from triglyceride-oil dosing → [Patrick, 2019]

#### (Membrane incorporation and synaptic signalling)

DHA integrates into phospholipid bilayers of neuronal membranes, influencing membrane fluidity, receptor dynamics, and synaptic signalling competence. Incorporation builds over weeks to months of habitual intake rather than through single-meal bolus exposure → [McNamara & Carlson, 2006]

#### (Phospholipid-bound delivery efficacy)

Phospholipid-bound DHA showed higher gray-matter accretion than triglyceride DHA in neonatal piglets — about 1.9-fold in that comparison. The contrast is animal delivery form, not a human capsule rule and not a choline-intake test → [Liu et al., 2014]

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This mechanism governs phospholipid-carrier delivery through neuronal-membrane incorporation over habitual intake. Lipid-mediator resolution biology belongs with inflammation-domain mechanisms. Acute amino-acid substrate supply is handled by [BRS1-FM1-PM1 - Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation). Large-neutral-amino-acid competition at the barrier belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM2 - LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation). Choline-to-acetylcholine conversion is a different choline fate, represented by [BRS1-FM2-PM6 - Acetylcholine Synthesis Support](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support). APOE4-sensitive delivery interpretation is handled by [BRS1(SM-SNP2)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/sm/brs1-sm-snp2-apoe4-omega-3-brain-delivery-sensitivity). Membrane PUFA protection and eicosanoid/SPM balance belong downstream with lipid-peroxidation control and eicosanoid–SPM balance.

#### (Integration within BRS1)

This mechanism operationalises membrane DHA incorporation within [BRS1(FM3)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-phospholipid-mediated-dha-delivery-and-membrane-integration). Habitual DHA provision and phospholipid/LPC delivery context remain the primary biological levers discussed here.

</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Brain DHA replacement and supplement claims</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

In 14 healthy adults, intravenous tracer PET and plasma measurements yielded an estimated **3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day** of whole-brain DHA incorporation (mean ± SD). This measures replacement from circulating DHA; it is **not the amount to eat or take as a supplement** Umhau et al. (2009) [[8]](#pm-ref-8).

Using a previously reported **5 g brain DHA pool**, rather than measuring that stock in the participants, the authors estimated **0.076% daily turnover** and a **911-day half-life (about 2.5 years)**. These steady-state estimates do not establish an optimal oral dose, the proportion of a capsule reaching the brain, or clinical benefit. Absorption, peripheral metabolism and delivery form separate swallowed DHA from brain incorporation. In the 14 healthy adults studied, estimated whole-brain DHA incorporation averaged **3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day**. Under steady-state assumptions, this represents net replacement of a few milligrams daily: **3.8 − 1.7 = 2.1 mg/day** and **3.8 + 1.7 = 5.5 mg/day**, or approximately **2–6 mg/day** after rounding. This is a descriptive mean ± one standard deviation, not the observed minimum–maximum range, a recommended replacement range or a dietary intake target Umhau et al. (2009) [[8]](#pm-ref-8).

**DHA is one part of brain lipid biology.** Human PET also measures incorporation of the omega-6 fatty acid arachidonic acid Giovacchini et al. (2002) [[9]](#pm-ref-9). Developing neuronal and glial cultures demonstrate local cholesterol synthesis and uptake Genaro-Mattos et al. (2019) [[10]](#pm-ref-10). These are distinct lipid processes, not evidence that additional supplements are required. This PM remains specific to DHA incorporation; the cholesterol culture study does not establish a dietary cholesterol requirement.

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

[Scientific Findings and their assessments are available in Evidence & Audit](?review=1#scientific-findings).

#### Summary

Human PET and plasma measurements estimated whole-brain DHA incorporation at 3.8 ± 1.7 mg/day; turnover and half-life estimates additionally used a previously reported brain DHA pool and steady-state assumptions. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) A porcine study found greater gray-matter DHA accretion from phospholipid-bound than triglyceride-bound DHA, consistent with reviewed carrier-dependent delivery biology. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) These findings establish measured incorporation and delivery-form relevance, without defining an optimal oral dose, capsule-to-brain transfer fraction or cognitive benefit.

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — Once DHA is in membranes it remains oxidisable; peroxidation control protects those polyunsaturated lipids but is not the incorporation step itself.
- [BRS3-FM3-PM8 — Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance) — Incorporated long-chain fats can feed eicosanoid and specialised pro-resolving mediator chemistry downstream of this membrane job.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS1-FM2-PM6 - Acetylcholine Synthesis Support](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support) — Converts choline plus acetyl-CoA into acetylcholine. That choline fate is transmitter synthesis, not phosphatidylcholine carriage of DHA for membrane incorporation.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM1 - Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) — Supplies circulating amino acids for monoamine precursors. Amino-acid pool adequacy is not DHA transport or membrane accretion.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM2 - LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) — Governs competitive brain entry of large neutral amino acids. LAT1 amino-acid competition is not MFSD2A LPC-DHA transport.
